title: Electron Spin Notation (↑ ↓) & Shell Mapping Matrices
topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Arrowhead vector notation:** electrons are drawn as arrowheads — an upward arrow (↑) represents spin +½ (clockwise) and a downward arrow (↓) represents spin −½ (anticlockwise); each box (orbital) can hold at most two arrows of opposite direction.

**Net zero paired magnetic field cancellation:** when an orbital contains two electrons with opposite spins, their magnetic moments are equal and opposite, so the net magnetic field of the pair is zero — the atom as a whole becomes diamagnetic for that pair.

**K shell complete mapping matrix:** the K shell (n = 1) contains only the single 1s orbital; it is filled as 1s¹ (one ↑) for hydrogen and 1s² (↑↓) for helium, where the pair is fully spin-compensated.

**L shell complete mapping matrix:** the L shell (n = 2) contains the 2s orbital plus three 2p orbitals (2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z). Filling follows Hund's rule — electrons first occupy each orbital singly with parallel spins before pairing: e.g. oxygen (1s² 2s² 2p⁴) shows one paired 2p box (↑↓) and two half-filled boxes (↑, ↑).

**Arrow direction convention:** in electron configuration notation the order of filling is drawn left-to-right across the orbitals of the subshell, and the last electron added determines the arrow direction for half-filled orbitals.

**M shell complete mapping matrix:** the M shell (n = 3) contains 3s (1 orbital), 3p (3 orbitals), and 3d (5 orbitals) = 9 orbitals total. For example, phosphorus (Z = 15) fills as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, with the three 3p electrons as ↑, ↑, ↑ in separate orbitals (half-filled stability).

**Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity:** for degenerate orbitals (same energy), electrons fill each orbital singly with parallel spins before any pairing occurs; this minimizes electron–electron repulsion and maximizes exchange energy stabilization.

**Aufbau (building-up) principle:** electrons are added to the lowest energy orbitals first, then to successively higher ones; the filling order is 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p → 5s → 4d → 5p → 6s → 4f → 5d → 6p → 7s → 5f → 6d → 7p.
**Diagonal rule for filling order:** the Aufbau filling sequence can be remembered using a diagonal chart — draw arrows diagonally upward-right through 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, etc.

**Subshell stability of half-filled and fully-filled:** half-filled (e.g., p³, d⁵) and fully-filled (e.g., p⁶, d¹⁰) subshells have extra stability due to symmetric electron distribution and maximum exchange energy; this explains exceptions like chromium (₁₆Cr³⁺ → [Ar] 3d³ 4s⁰ rather than 3d² 4s¹ in some cases, and Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ instead of 3d⁹ 4s²).

**Diamagnetic vs paramagnetic classification:** if all electrons are paired (↑↓ in every orbital), the substance is diamagnetic (weakly repelled by a magnetic field); if unpaired electrons exist, it is paramagnetic (attracted to a magnetic field). For example, O₂ has two unpaired electrons in its 2p orbitals, making it paramagnetic — a fact the Lewis structure fails to predict.

**Real-world application — MRI and NMR:** magnetic resonance imaging relies on the different spin states of hydrogen nuclei (protons) in a magnetic field; understanding electron spin notation extends naturally to nuclear spin, where paired nucleons have spin 0 and unpaired ones have spin ½.

**Neon complete mapping (full L shell):** neon (Z = 10): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ — all orbitals filled, all spins paired, completely stable noble gas configuration. Box diagram: [↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓].
confusion: Misconception: The arrow direction (↑ or ↓) represents the physical direction of electron travel. Correction — the arrows represent spin angular momentum orientation (mₛ = +½ or −½), not the direction the electron moves through space. The electron does not literally travel in circles like a spinning top.

Misconception: Hund's rule only applies to p orbitals. Correction — Hund's rule applies to ALL degenerate orbitals: p (3 orbitals), d (5 orbitals), and f (7 orbitals). For example, in the 3d subshell, the first five electrons each occupy a separate d-orbital with parallel spins before any pairing occurs.

Misconception: Paired electrons cancel each other out completely, so they don't matter. Correction — while paired electrons have zero net spin and zero net magnetic moment, they still contribute to the atom's total energy, chemical bonding, and shielding effects. The Pauli exclusion principle that forces them into different quantum states has profound structural consequences.

Misconception: The filling order is always strictly 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 3d → 4s → ... . Correction — the 4s orbital fills before 3d (4s is lower in energy than 3d for neutral atoms), so the order is ...3p → 4s → 3d → 4p. However, after filling, when transition metal ions lose electrons, they lose 4s electrons first.
practice: Draw the complete box orbital diagram for oxygen (Z = 8). Solution: 1s: [↑↓], 2s: [↑↓], 2p: [↑↓][↑][↑]. Total electrons = 2+2+4 = 8. Two unpaired electrons in 2p orbitals → paramagnetic.

Write the electron configuration and box diagram for iron (Z = 26). Solution: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Box diagram: 4s [↑↓], 3d [↑↓][↑][↑][↑][↑]. Four unpaired 3d electrons → paramagnetic. Note: the 4s fills before 3d per Aufbau.

Identify which of the following violate Hund's rule, Pauli exclusion principle, or Aufbau principle: (a) 1s² 2s² 2p⁵, (b) 1s³, (c) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ 3p⁵. Solution: (b) 1s³ violates Pauli — only 2 electrons fit in 1s. (c) 3p⁵ before 3s¹ is complete violates Aufbau — 3s must fill before 3p. (a) is valid.

Explain why nitrogen (Z = 7) is more stable than one might expect, and why Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ instead of [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s². Solution: Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p³ subshell with one electron in each of the three 2p orbitals — this symmetric arrangement maximizes exchange energy. Chromium similarly gains stability by achieving a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell, so one 4s electron promotes to 3d, giving [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.
universalFacts: Oxygen is paramagnetic (attracted to magnetic fields) despite having all paired electrons in many Lewis structures — this was a major triumph of quantum mechanical orbital theory over classical bonding models.

The complete electron configuration of every known element follows the same Aufbau filling order, with only a few exceptions (Cr, Cu, Mo, Ag, etc.) that are explained by half-filled and fully-filled subshell stability.

The Pauli exclusion principle, formulated by Wolfgang Pauli in 1925, not only explains shell structure but also why matter has volume — electrons cannot all collapse into the same lowest-energy state.

The notation ↑↓ in a single box means two electrons share the same spatial orbital (same n, l, mₗ) but differ in spin (mₛ = +½ vs −½) — this is the only way to satisfy the Pauli exclusion principle while maximizing the number of electrons per orbital.
